questions.q: What is the hard ceiling for a VARCHAR(n) with a specific numeric length?
options: 8,000 characters
255 characters
50 characters
There is no limit for a numeric length
questions.explain: Beyond 8,000 characters, you need VARCHAR(MAX) instead of a specific numeric length.

questions.q: Roughly how much text can VARCHAR(MAX) store?
options: Up to about 2 GB — practically unlimited
Exactly 8,000 characters, same as regular VARCHAR
Up to 100 characters
Unlimited, with no storage engine differences at all
questions.explain: VARCHAR(MAX) is designed for content with no realistic upper bound, like article bodies or descriptions.

questions.q: Why shouldn't you just declare every text column as VARCHAR(MAX)?
options: A specific declared length documents the expected size, and large MAX values can be stored off-row with real performance implications
VARCHAR(MAX) cannot store any text at all
VARCHAR(MAX) is deprecated and should never be used
VARCHAR(MAX) columns cannot be queried with WHERE
questions.explain: Using MAX everywhere loses the documentation value of a bounded length and can have storage engine performance implications.

options: The Unicode equivalent of VARCHAR(MAX) — unlimited-length text with full Unicode support
A synonym for VARCHAR(MAX) with no actual difference
A fixed-length Unicode type
A numeric data type for very large numbers
questions.explain: Same relationship as VARCHAR/NVARCHAR from Lesson 42, just applied to the MAX-length variant.

questions.q: What should you use instead of the old TEXT data type in new T-SQL code?
options: VARCHAR(MAX), since TEXT is deprecated
CHAR(MAX)
TEXT is still the recommended choice for new code
INT
questions.explain: TEXT was replaced by VARCHAR(MAX) years ago and should be avoided in new development.
